articles.raw_description: In the beginning, my garage door opener worked fine. When the door opened or closed, I would get a notification. If I'm away from home and the door opens, so... Garage Door Spam 16 Nov, 2026 In the beginning, my garage door opener worked fine. When the door opened or closed, I would get a notification. If I'm away from home and the door opens, something weird is going down. The "myQ" app generally worked although it was encrusted with ads: I continued using it because I trusted that notifications were meaningful... ...until recently (October 2026): This is un-fucking-acceptable. As in, absolutely fucking not. The manufacturer (Chamberlain) cut off third-party access to its APIs (via myQ) in late 2023. In response, I purchased a pair of ratgdo32 devices to opt out of the bullshit. ratgdo is a WiFi control board for your garage door opener that works over your local network using ESP Home or HomeKit The device is a ~$62 board from ratcloud llc running open-source firmware that wires to the opener's existing terminals and speaks LiftMaster's Security+ 2.0 protocol locally. These were easy enough to hook up. I won't reproduce the instructions here. The bundle included six black wires, an auxiliary harness I didn’t need. My router hands each board a fixed address at 192.168.0.192 and 192.168.0.245. articles.title: Pancreatic cancer halted by virus injection in three patients
articles.raw_description: A cancer-killing virus has stopped pancreatic tumours from growing and spreading in three people in an initial safety trial, raising hopes that it may help to beat the deadly condition A scanning electron micrograph of pancreatic cancer cells ANNE WESTON, EM STP, THE FRANCIS CRICK INSTITUTE/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY A virus has stopped pancreatic cancer in its tracks in three people in a clinical trial in the US. Further evaluation is needed in larger trials, but the early results are encouraging, especially since only small doses of the virus were administered for initial safety testing. “We only injected one-tenth of the dose we are eventually aiming at, so the efficacy is better than I expected, especially as this is pancreatic cancer,” says Masato Yamamoto at the University of Minnesota, who led the development of the viral treatment. Read more Woman in cancer remission without treatment in highly unusual case Pancreatic cancer is notorious for being the deadliest type of the condition. One reason is that symptoms tend to appear late, when the cancer has already spread and cannot be surgically removed. Once diagnosed, people usually live only around three to six months . Advertisement Another reason is that pancreatic tumours have tough, fibrous exteriors that block chemotherapy drugs from getting in. “They’re hard as hockey pucks,” says Yamamoto. articles.title: Claude solves two open problems in the physics of black holes
articles.raw_description: Claude Fable 5.2 has solved two open problems in theoretical physics. Both concern black holes and the search for a theory of quantum gravity. 01 Introduction Claude has solved two open problems in theoretical physics. Both concern black holes and the search for a theory of quantum gravity. In the first, it completed a calculation that physicists set up more than 20 years ago, but which had never been solved. Claude’s result showed that a sudden transition associated with the formation of black holes persists even where spacetime no longer has a definite shape. In the second, Claude found the exact limit of the simplest version of a technique used to test candidate theories of quantum gravity. This post explains both findings, first in plain terms and then in more technical detail. The preprints are available here and here . Introduction Modern physics rests on two frameworks: general relativity and quantum mechanics. General relativity describes very large things, like stars; quantum mechanics describes very small things, such as atoms. Both are astonishingly good at predicting how the universe behaves, but they’re mathematically incompatible. Finding a theory that unites them—“quantum gravity”—is one of the field’s biggest goals. Black holes are a natural testing ground, because they’re one of the few areas where both relativity and quantum mechanics matter—they pack immense mass into a very small space. articles.title: How to CAD Almost Anything
articles.raw_description: Have you ever wondered how objects from our daily lives are designed? How can we generate a computer 3D model of a mug, a bottle of Diet Coke, or a Saturn V rocket? What about designing the blades of a jet engine? A test dummy? How about making an animation of a LEGO house building itself? Or making a realistic render of a bowl of fruit? In this workshop, you will learn skills to design all these and much more! How to CAD Almost Anything introduces students to CAD (Computer-Aided Design) through various fun examples focused on reverse engineering. In contrast to traditional mechanical design courses, this workshop emphasizes the design process itself, understanding how to plan and best leverage our available tools to arrive at our desired result. Thus, the sessions are less about following the instructions on an engineering drawing and more about independent thinking and strategizing, such as reverse engineering an object into a 3D model. Come and learn how to CAD almost anything! articles.title: OpenSSL: Buffer overflow in EVP_EncodeBlock() (CVE-2026-121481, CVSS 9.8)
articles.raw_description: This fixes "Buffer overflow in EVP_EncodeBlock()" (CVE-2026-121481) by returning -1 for invalid inputs to EVP_EncodeBlock(): NULL input or output buffers, negative lengths, and lengths fo... Conversation nmouha commented Nov 10, 2026 Copy link Copy Markdown Contributor This fixes "Buffer overflow in EVP_EncodeBlock()" ( CVE-2026-121481 ) by returning -1 for invalid inputs to EVP_EncodeBlock() : NULL input or output buffers, negative lengths, and lengths for which the encoded size does not fit in an int . The OpenSSL SRT has asked for it to be fixed publicly; the advisory is still pending. Returning -1 for invalid inputs is the most straightforward fix, and matches what happens in wolfSSL's compatibility layer for OpenSSL's EVP_EncodeBlock() . I'm suggesting a similar guard for EVP_DecodeBlock() . No length limit is needed here because the decoded length always fits in an int , but it is a good idea to reject NULL buffers and negative lengths. Moreover, I propose to fix the incorrect length check in the base64encode() function of http_client.c , which rejected only len > INT_MAX . I am adding tests in test/base64_dec_avx2_test.c to cover the new behavior, and documenting the -1 returns in doc/man3/EVP_EncodeInit.pod . Exploiting this vulnerability from the command line is possible by passing a large -proxy_pass to openssl s_client . I confirmed that GOST accepts these large passwords out of the box. articles.title: Vint Cerf on why TCP/IP was never patented
articles.raw_description: Future Stories, my new podcast about technology, science and the way we live, starts today. The first guest is one of the people who built the Internet. Vint Cerf on why TCP/IP was never patented Future Stories, my new podcast about technology, science and the way we live, starts today. The first guest is one of the people who built the Internet. João Tomé Nov 19, 2026 1 Share EXTRA, extra! Today I’m launching Future Stories, my own podcast about technology, science and the way we live. The first guest is Vint Cerf . He co-designed TCP/IP with Bob Kahn in the 1970s, the rules that let the world’s networks talk to each other. Interviewing him was on my bucket list for years. When I was at Cloudflare I thought about asking him many times, but I was a bit shy. He’s Vint Cerf, after all. This year I finally asked, and he said yes. We talked over Zoom (not using Zoom again) on October 14. He’s 83, he left Google this year after more than twenty years, and he’s helping start a company, Tolero, that is building software for an Internet between planets. His words: “the speed of light is too slow.” “Who will our allies be 25 years from now? And we didn’t know. So we thought the only way we can be assured that the allies will have access to this is to simply open it up.” Some peculiar stories from the conversation First, a bug related one (ring a bell? those never stopped over the years…) .
